runs: Beyond the business, PLAZA's ESG approach cuts across its decisions and aims, besides contributing to sustainable development, to access financial benefits both of its own and from external sources. Bloomberg rates the company at 3.39 points, below the global industry average (5–6 points) and below its direct competitors in Chile (Figure E1); this is partly offset by its local “green” profile, as it ranks among the leading real estate companies in the region.
Potential financial benefits:

in operations, the energy management system (EnMS) certified under ISO 50001 improves energy performance and lowers operating costs. Among local external benefits: Peru recognizes the company with 2 of 4 stars in “Huella de Carbono Perú”, which eases permits and licenses; and Colombia, under Law 2099 of 2021, grants income-tax deductions for environmental investments. The company also holds certifications and belongs to indices such as DJSI MILA (Figure E1).

Figure E6 estimates, as a scenario and not as data, that operating ESG savings add about CLP 2 per share and that a 25 bp cut in the cost of debt and equity would add CLP 72 per share, against the CLP 1,478 gap between the target price and the share price. The ESG effect on value is therefore marginal; what matters for the thesis is corporate governance (see below).

PLAZA's approach is efficient, sustainable and circular operational management based on continuous improvement in environmental performance, which translates into lower operating costs. It has three focus areas: energy and water efficiency, carbon footprint, and waste management. Its main objective is carbon neutrality: Net Zero in direct and indirect emissions by 2035 (65.6% progress in 2025).
Energy:

reduce the energy intensity of common-area expenses by 22% by 2035 (35.5% progress in 2025; Figure E2) and reach 100% renewable electricity in 2026 (89.3% progress). In 2025, annual consumption was 0.16 MWh/m² of GLA, of which 0.14 renewable and 0.014 non-renewable (Figure E3).
Water:
reduce direct water consumption by 30% by 2025, achieved at 100.9%, helped by its LEED and EDGE certifications; in 2025, average annual consumption was 0.77 m³/m² of GLA and 0.66 m³/m² in December.
HCFC:

eliminate 100% of HCFC use by 2030 (14.9% progress in 2025), key to GHG emissions management, an area in which Bloomberg recognizes PLAZA as a global industry leader (a component separate from the total ESG score).
Waste:

recover 60% of the waste generated in 2025 (46.2% recovered, 77% of the target; Figure E3 and Appendix [Y], Figure S4) and divert 75% of solid waste from landfills by 2027; it reports having eliminated 97% of single-use plastics.
Climate management:

it adopts the TCFD recommendations to integrate physical and transition risks, with environmental due diligence on acquisitions, under a compliance program aligned with ISO 14001 and monitored by the sustainability committee.

The social dimension is built on a model of long-term ethical relationships (Appendix [Y], Figure S3) and shared value creation that places stakeholders at the center, aligned with ISO 45001 and ILO guidelines; in 2025 the risk detection and response program of the human rights policy was added. PLAZA engages its stakeholders through community dialogues, materiality assessments and organizational culture surveys (Appendix [Y], section 5), and has an integrity hotline for social incidents; CADEM ranked it 31st of 385 “Marcas Ciudadanas” (“Citizen Brands”) and first in the “Shopping Centers” category (2026). Employees receive training and programs for those nearing retirement, and suppliers are evaluated with sustainability criteria (55.3% of regional and 38.4% of foreign suppliers). With tenants it maintains a relationship model centered on value proposition and experience; their satisfaction, measured by NPS, rose to 13 points in 2025 (Figure E4). Each center has emergency manuals and runs drills (52 in 2025), and PLAZA implemented ISO/IEC 27001 for information security.

On diversity, women are 53.2% of the workforce and hold 42% of management positions (Figure E4), but a gender pay gap of 28% on average regionally persists and the Board has only one woman among 9 directors. The target for 2028 is for 60% of the properties to be certified as inclusive spaces, and PLAZA obtained the “Sello Mayor” (“Senior Seal”) at one of its centers, the first in Chile, which certifies physical and operational adaptation for older adults. As it expands, building to those parameters avoids future retrofitting costs and allows the transition of existing centers to begin.

Corporate governance is guided by the G20 and OECD principles and aligned with the CMF's NCG 461, with the aim of ensuring transparency, risk control and monitoring of the strategy and of ESG commitments.
Board and committees:

the Board has 9 members and only one is independent (below 50%), which creates agency risk (Figure E5 and Appendix [Y], Figure S2) and is the only unfavorable factor in the ESG risk matrix (Appendix [Y], Figure S5). It defines objectives, strategy and policies; the directors' committee (3 members) reviews the financial statements and mitigates agency risks, and both oversee the risk management led by the executive committee and the CEO. In the second half of 2025, CEO Fernando de Peña Iver resigned effective at year-end, and Pablo Pulido Sierra took over in 2026.
Executive compensation:
33.3% of executives' variable pay depends on ESG KPIs and 61% on non-financial metrics (Figure E5), which aligns incentives with ESG goals.
Shareholders:

control is concentrated: Falabella S.A., through Desarrollos Inmobiliarios SpA, holds 53.1% of the shares (Appendix [Y], Figure S1); minority shareholders holding 1% may propose director candidates, and the shareholders' meeting elects the Board and external auditors and approves the dividend policy.
Ethics, audits and controls:

the integrity code and the crime prevention model guide conduct; PLAZA operates the Autocompliance platform (meetings with public officials, gifts and invitations) and a confidential integrity hotline. In 2025 it reported regional non-compliance cases and complaints related to workers and customers, but none concerning corruption or conduct that undermines market development (Appendix [Y], section 3). The directors' committee oversees an internal audit that reports to it monthly and appoints the external auditors and credit rating agencies.
Relevance for the thesis:

governance matters, not ESG savings. With Falabella as controller, related companies contributing 15.7% of revenue and a board with a single independent director, the question is whether expansion, whose return is below its cost of capital, benefits the controller more than minority shareholders (see Valuation and Risks, RR1).
